evidence.title: Agent-management work grows as human attention becomes a bottleneck
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: Anthropic reports that agent-management and meta-work rose from 10% to 22% of interactive sessions. Its interviews and output-reading estimates identify human attention as a bottleneck in an organization using AI extensively. Observation period and measurement context: Several series through August 2026; session comparison fall 2025 to spring 2026.
evidence.evidence_standing: Source-reported bounded account; study or measurement; not independently reproduced
evidence.glossary_fit: Illustrative or qualifying; does not validate a definition

source_locations.SRC-123: Productivity and human-attention bottleneck sections; figure notes and methods

evidence.limitations: Single rapidly growing developer; nonrandom adoption. Estimated reading demand is not observed reading time. Human communication and executive control persisted. Neither oversight failure nor general labor-market effects are established.
evidence.open_questions: Transfer to other populations, tasks and operating environments remains unestablished. Missing measurement details are not inferred.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: Supervision is work with its own attention requirements; this does not establish that intervention failed.
evidence.dispute_status: See source version and dispute qualifications; no systematic clearance claimed.
evidence.verification_status: Not independently verified by the Commons

terms.name: Chaperoning
terms.definition: The continuing supervisory activity of independently observing consequential behavior, exercising informed judgment, and intervening effectively when appropriate. This requires access, competence, authority, and an actual ability to alter outcomes—not nominal participation or an agent merely stating that an action is inappropriate.

relationships.explanation: Illustrates attention and assessment demands of supervision; not a demonstration of ineffective oversight.
